37:4.text: And I saw another angel fly in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting gospel to preach unto them that dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people,

provenance.other: “nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 14:6, and “the everlasting gospel” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The fourfold list is Revelation's signature — 5:9, 7:9, 11:9, 13:7, 14:6 — but only at 14:6 does it stand in the Book of Mormon's order and syntax, governed by a verb of going forth. Daniel 3:4 and 7:14 have a threefold 'people, nations, and languages' with no kindreds.
provenance.significance: The angel of Revelation 14:6 does not carry a message; he carries a book — 'the everlasting gospel', a KJV singleton — and flies with it to the four categories of the earth. Alma 37:4 has the plates of brass 'kept and preserved by the hand of the Lord, until they should go forth unto every nation, kindred, tongue and people'. The Book of Mormon has given the angel's itinerary to an object, and to an object which its own nineteenth-century readers would meet as a book brought by an angel. The metalepsis runs the right way: recover Revelation 14:6 and the record Alma is handing his son is already, in the source, airborne.

37:4.note: The catalogue adjudicates this formula first at 1 Nephi 5:18, where the plates of brass are likewise its subject; the argument is made there and is not restated. It is given as a link rather than a recurrence because Alma is a new book and a new hand (CONVENTIONS/ADJUDICATING §4, ratified 2026-09-05), and because Alma 37:4 restores the 1 Nephi 5:18 setting exactly — the same plates, the same going forth, the same four categories — after thirty-five chapters in which the formula has drifted into general use. The 1830 'nation, kindred, tongue and people' is singular throughout, as Revelation 14:6 is; the plural 'kindreds, and tongues' of Revelation 7:9 is not what is being copied.

37:6.text: But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;

provenance.other: “confound the wise” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 1:27, which is also the only KJV verse with 'the foolish things of the world' and 'the weak things of the world'.
provenance.significance: The catalogue has met 'confound the wise' before, at Alma 32:23, where three words were borrowed and the argument around them was Alma's own. Here the argument is Paul's as well. 1 Corinthians 1:18-27 runs: the preaching of the cross is foolishness to them that perish; it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe; the weakness of God is stronger than men; God hath chosen the foolish and the weak things of the world to confound the wise and the mighty. Alma 37:6-7 runs: you may suppose this is foolishness in me; by small and simple things are great things brought to pass; small means doth confound the wise; and by very small means the Lord bringeth about the salvation of many souls. Paul's four moves in Paul's order, with 'small' substituted throughout for 'foolish' and 'weak'. The substitution is the finding: Alma is defending an object — a set of plates that looks trivial — where Paul was defending a message that sounded absurd, and 'small' is the term that transfers the argument from a proposition to a thing.

37:6.note: 'Now ye may suppose that this is foolishness in me; but behold I say unto you, That by small and simple things, are great things brought to pass; and small means, in many instances, doth confound the wise.' The KJV singleton is the hinge, and the sentence that precedes it names foolishness while the sentence that follows it names the salvation of souls — which is 1 Corinthians 1:21's 'by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe'. The whole borrowing falls well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his passages; it is a compressed argument, not a quotation. Filed at 37:6 with 37:7 in recurrence because 37:7 repeats 'confound the wise' with the substituted term ('very small means') made explicit.

37:8.text: Let him know, that he which converteth the sinner from the error of his way shall save a soul from death, and shall hide a multitude of sins.

provenance.other: “the error of his way” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “save a soul from death” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and both are James 5:20, in the same clause. 'Salvation of souls' occurs in no KJV verse at all — the Book of Mormon's noun phrase is a nominalisation of James's verb.
provenance.significance: James 5:19-20 is the last sentence of the epistle and its subject is the one office Alma is handing over: not preaching to the world but turning back a brother who has erred. Recover it and the promise attached is startling for the setting — the converter saves a soul from death 'and shall hide a multitude of sins'. Alma is describing what the records have already done to the Lamanites (37:9) and what he expects them to do to 'our stiffnecked brethren, the Nephites' (37:10), who are precisely the erring insiders James has in view. The plates are being cast as the agent of James's final imperative.

37:8.note: 'They have enlarged the memory of this people, yea, and convinced many of the error of their ways, and brought them to the knowledge of their God, unto the salvation of their souls.' Two KJV singletons from one verse, in that verse's order — convincing a man of the error of his way, and the saving of the soul — with James's singular pronouns pluralised to fit a people. The clause between them, 'brought them to the knowledge of their God', is the Book of Mormon's own; James has 'converteth', which Alma reserves for the parallel sentence at 37:9 ('brought them unto repentance; that is, they brought them to the knowledge of the Lord their God'). The verse was invisible to the n-gram stream, which proposed nothing at all here.

37:15.text: And the Lord said, Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat:

provenance.route: Luke 22:31 → KJV → Book of Mormon, with Psalm 35:5 supplying the substituted object
provenance.other: “sift you as” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 22:31, and “as chaff before the wind” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 35:5. 'Delivered up unto Satan' answers to 1 Corinthians 5:5, 'to deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh' — the KJV's only handing of a person over to Satan as a disciplinary act.
provenance.significance: The substitution is the whole finding. Luke 22:31 is spoken to Peter on the night of the betrayal and its threat is survivable by design: sifting wheat is what separates wheat from chaff, and Christ's next words are 'I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not; and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren'. Alma keeps Luke's clause word for word and replaces its object with the Psalter's — 'sift you as chaff before the wind', where Psalm 35:5 asks that the wicked be chased away by the angel of the LORD, and Psalm 1:4 makes chaff the figure of the ungodly. The sifted man in Luke is the one who survives sifting; the sifted man in Alma is the residue that blows away. Alma is warning a son who is about to receive the records, and he has taken the Bible's one consoling sentence about Satanic sifting and removed the consolation from it by changing one noun.

37:15.note: 'Ye shall be delivered up unto satan, that he may sift you as chaff before the wind.' Six words are Luke 22:31's and are found nowhere else in the KJV; the four that follow are Psalm 35:5's and are found nowhere else in the KJV. The construction is Luke's exactly — 'that he may sift you as' — so the fusion happens at the last word, which is where the sense turns. The preceding clause, 'ye shall be delivered up unto satan', is 1 Corinthians 5:5's disciplinary formula, so all three of the sentence's elements are borrowed and each from a different testament. Compare Hays on metalepsis: the reader who does not recover Luke 22:31 loses the fact that a promise has been converted into a threat.

37:21.text: And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them.

provenance.other: “works of darkness” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Ephesians 5:11 and Romans 13:12. Romans has it in an armour-and-daylight figure with nothing secret about it; Ephesians has it in a passage about secrecy and disclosure. 'Made manifest' is common (nineteen verses) and carries no weight on its own.
provenance.alternative: Luke 8:17, 'nothing is secret, that shall not be made manifest', is the tighter match for the two words 'secret' and 'manifest' considered alone, and a reader who wants a single verse rather than a window should take it.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 5:11-13 is the New Testament's one sustained treatment of the problem Alma 37:21-29 is actually facing: what to do with a record of secret wickedness. Paul's three moves are reprove the works of darkness (11), do not so much as speak of the things done in secret (12), and let the light make them manifest (13). Alma's are make the murders and abominations manifest to this people (21, 29), retain their oaths and covenants and signs so that the people never learn them (27), and let the Lord's stone bring the secret works out of darkness into light (23-25). He has taken all three of Paul's moves and separated what Paul left joined — the wickedness is published, the method is suppressed. That distinction is not in Ephesians, and it is the chapter's own contribution.

37:21.note: 'That the mysteries and the works of darkness, and their secret works, or the secret works of those people, which have been destroyed, may be made manifest unto this people.' No single phrase here is decisive, which is why this is filed as an echo at moderate; what argues for it is that a three-verse window in Ephesians supplies all three of the verse's terms in the verse's order, and that the same window governs Alma's next eight verses. Note the 1830 'directors' at the end of the verse, changed to 'interpreters' in 1920 — the object under discussion is renamed between editions, though nothing in the biblical contact depends on it.
37:21.whyNot: The verbal contact is one two-verse phrase ('works of darkness') plus two common words. If the Book of Mormon simply inherited 'works of darkness' as ordinary religious English — which by 1830 it plainly was — the Ephesians window explains nothing that the Romans 13:12 phrase does not.

37:23.text: He discovereth deep things out of darkness, and bringeth out to light the shadow of death.

provenance.other: “discovereth deep things out of darkness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Job 12:22, which is also the KJV's only pairing of the verb 'discover' in its old sense — uncover, disclose — with a movement from darkness to light.
provenance.significance: Job 12:13-25 is Job's ironic hymn to a wisdom that undoes governments: God 'leadeth counsellors away spoiled', 'looseth the bond of kings', 'poureth contempt upon princes', 'taketh away the heart of the chief of the people of the earth' — and, at 12:22, discovers deep things out of darkness. Alma is describing a stone given so that a secret conspiracy inside a nation can be exposed and, in the event, so that the nation destroyed by it can be catalogued. The passage he has reached for is the Bible's one description of God as the discoverer of what political darkness conceals, and Job's list of what that discovery does to rulers is the fate of the people whose record the stone reads.

37:23.note: 'I will prepare unto my servant Gazelem, a stone, which shall shine forth in darkness unto light, that I may discover unto my people which serve me, that I may discover unto them the works of their brethren; yea, their secret works, their works of darkness.' 'Discover' is used twice and in the KJV's obsolete transitive sense, which by 1829 was archaic English and is the mark of the borrowing; the darkness-to-light movement attached to it is Job 12:22's, in Job 12:22's order. Held at moderate because the shared content words are two and the construction is not reproduced. The link is filed here rather than at 37:25 because 'discover' is the word only Job supplies; 37:25 repeats the darkness-to-light clause and is adjudicated separately to 1 Corinthians 4:5, which supplies what Job does not.

37:25.text: Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come, who both will bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts: and then shall every man have praise of God.

provenance.other: “bring to light” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “hidden things of darkness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and both are 1 Corinthians 4:5, where they stand in the order Alma 37:25 uses them.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is an instruction to withhold judgment: judge nothing before the time, because the Lord's coming is what will bring the hidden things of darkness to light. Alma 37:25 is the divine speech that the Jaredite record fulfils, and 37:26 reports the fulfilment — 'thus far the word of God hath been fulfilled; yea, their secret abominations have been brought out of darkness'. The Book of Mormon has taken the eschatological clause out of Paul's prohibition and made it a completed act of publication inside history, discharged by a translated record rather than by the Lord's coming. What Paul defers, Alma reports as done; and what Alma has in hand is the book his own reader is holding.

37:25.note: 'I will bring forth out of darkness unto light, all their secret works and their abominations … and I will bring to light all their secrets and abominations, unto every nation that shall hereafter possess the land.' Two KJV singletons from a single verse, in that verse's sequence, and the surrounding vocabulary of 37:21-26 — 'made manifest', the works of darkness, the secret things — is 1 Corinthians 4:5's remaining clause ('will make manifest the counsels of the hearts') distributed across the passage. The closing phrase 'unto every nation that shall hereafter possess the land' returns the divine speech to the going-forth of 37:4, so the two ends of the chapter's argument about records are both worded out of the New Testament's language for eschatological disclosure.

37:28.text: And another angel came out from the altar, which had power over fire; and cried with a loud cry to him that had the sharp sickle, saying, Thrust in thy sharp sickle, and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth; for her grapes are fully ripe.

provenance.other: “fully ripe” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 14:18; Joel 3:13, the verse Revelation is reworking, reads 'for the harvest is ripe' without the adverb.
provenance.significance: Revelation 14:18-20 is the vintage of wrath: the grapes are gathered when fully ripe and cast into the winepress, and blood comes out of the press to the horses' bridles. Alma's clause is a timing rule for national destruction — the curse falls on the workers of darkness 'when they are fully ripe', and 37:31 repeats it as the condition that can still be escaped, 'except they repent before they are fully ripe'. What the Book of Mormon takes from Revelation is not the imagery, which it drops entirely, but the adverb: ripeness that is not yet full is the interval in which repentance is possible, and that interval exists in the source only as the moment before the sickle is thrust in.
provenance.alternative: By Alma the phrase is a Book of Mormon formula in its own right (2 Nephi 28:16, and forward to Alma 45:16 and Ether), so the proximate model may be internal rather than biblical.

37:28.note: The catalogue adjudicates the phrase first at 2 Nephi 28:16 and the argument for the KJV singleton is made there. The row is given here rather than passed over because Alma is a different book and a different hand (ADJUDICATING §4), and because Alma 37:28-31 does something 2 Nephi 28:16 does not: it turns the adverb into a condition with an escape clause, twice, and makes it the ground of a request ('therefore I desire that this people might not be destroyed'). Moderate rather than high because the verbal contact is two words and by this point in the corpus the phrase is plainly internal currency.

37:34.text: Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.

provenance.other: “meek and lowly in heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “rest unto your souls” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and both are Matthew 11:29. Jeremiah 6:16, which Matthew is reworking, has 'ye shall find rest for your souls'.
provenance.significance: Matthew 11:28-30 is an invitation issued by Christ in the first person — come unto me, take my yoke, learn of me, for I am meek and lowly in heart. Alma converts every first person in it to a third: teach them to be meek and lowly in heart, for such shall find rest to their souls. The self-description becomes a curriculum, and the promise that in Matthew is attached to a person ('rest unto your souls' follows 'learn of me') is here attached to a disposition. That is a considerable theological move made entirely by changing pronouns, and it is the third time in six chapters that Alma has taken a piece of this verse — 'lowly in heart' at 32:8, 'learn of me' at 36:3, the yoke's ease at 33:23 — without ever quoting it whole. Here he quotes it whole.

37:34.note: 'Teach them to never be weary of good works, but to be meek and lowly in heart: for such shall find rest to their souls.' Two KJV singletons in Matthew's own order and with Matthew's own connective ('for'), which is what lifts this above the partial borrowings the catalogue has already filed at Alma 32:8, 33:23 and 36:3 and is why it is a fresh link rather than a recurrence of them (ADJUDICATING §4). Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his passages. `mediation-check.py` on Jeremiah 6:16 against Matthew 11:29 returns two decisive points for Matthew and none for Jeremiah — Alma has the meekness and lowliness that only Matthew supplies, and none of Jeremiah's old paths — so the route is the Gospel, not the prophet. One departure is worth recording: Alma reads 'rest TO their souls' where Matthew has 'unto your souls' and Jeremiah has 'for your souls', a third preposition belonging to neither.

37:35.text: Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth; and let thy heart cheer thee in the days of thy youth, and walk in the ways of thine heart, and in the sight of thine eyes: but know thou, that for all these things God will bring thee into judgment.

provenance.other: “in thy youth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ecclesiastes 11:9, which also carries the near variant 'in the days of thy youth' — repeated at 12:1. 'Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth' (12:1) and 'Fear God, and keep his commandments' (12:13) are the epilogue's opening and closing imperatives.
provenance.significance: Read Alma 37:35-36 against Ecclesiastes 11:9 and it is a rebuttal, clause by clause. Qoheleth: rejoice in thy youth, let thy heart cheer thee, walk in the ways of thine heart and in the sight of thine eyes — but know that God will bring thee into judgment. Alma: learn wisdom in thy youth, learn in thy youth to keep the commandments, let thy thoughts be directed unto the Lord, let the affections of thy heart be placed upon the Lord forever. The two verses share the singleton, the address to a young man, and the heart as the thing that must be pointed somewhere; they differ on where. Alma has kept Qoheleth's warning and deleted the permission that precedes it, and he has done to Ecclesiastes 11:9 what Ecclesiastes 12:1 already does to it — which is to say he has read the source's own self-correction and finished it.

37:35.note: 'O remember my son, and learn wisdom in thy youth; yea, learn in thy youth to keep the commandments of God.' The KJV singleton twice in one verse, opened by 'remember' (Ecclesiastes 12:1's imperative) and closed by 'keep the commandments' (12:13's). Three points of the Preacher's epilogue in eleven words, and the epilogue is the KJV's one address by an old teacher to a young man about what to do with his youth — which is the situation of Alma 37 exactly. The n-gram stream proposed Deuteronomy 10:13 here on 'keep the commandments of', which is boilerplate; the actual source shares only three content words and is invisible to a contiguous window (CONVENTIONS §9).

37:37.text: In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.

provenance.other: “he shall direct thy paths” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Proverbs 3:6. “when thou liest down” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Deuteronomy 6:7, Deuteronomy 11:19 and Proverbs 3:24 — and 'and when thou risest' in two of them, so the whole of Alma's day-and-night frame is drawn from those three verses and no others.
provenance.significance: Proverbs 3 is the KJV's model of the speech Alma 37 is: a father to a son, 'My son, forget not my law; but let thine heart keep my commandments' (3:1). Alma has used two widely separated verses of it in one sentence. Proverbs 3:6 supplies the conditional — acknowledge him in all thy ways and he will direct you — and Proverbs 3:24 supplies what happens at night: 'When thou liest down, thou shalt not be afraid: yea, thou shalt lie down, and thy sleep shall be sweet.' Between them the borrowing picks up Deuteronomy 6:7's Shema formula, 'when thou liest down, and when thou risest up', which is the KJV's phrase for the whole of a day's obedience. So the sentence that tells Helaman what to do with his waking and sleeping hours is assembled from the Bible's two places for saying it, the wisdom text and the covenant text, and the substitution of 'doings' for 'ways' is Alma's only word of his own in the frame.

37:37.note: 'Counsel the Lord in all thy doings, and he will direct thee for good; yea, when thou liest down at night, lie down unto the Lord, that he may watch over you in your sleep; and when thou risest in the morning, let thy heart be full of thanks unto God.' Proverbs 3:6's construction is kept intact — imperative, 'in all thy [x]', 'and he will direct thee' — with the object of the verb changed from the paths to the person, and 'ways' changed to 'doings'. Note that 37:36 has already used 'let all thy doings be unto the Lord', so the substituted noun is established a verse earlier; and note the reversal in the imperative itself, 'counsel the Lord' where Proverbs has the man acknowledging God. The 1830 reads 'watch over you in your sleep' with no preposition before 'sleep' in the following clause where 1920 supplies 'with'; nothing in the borrowing turns on it.

37:37.text: Wherefore the rather, brethren, give diligence to make your calling and election sure: for if ye do these things, ye shall never fall:

provenance.other: “if ye do these things, ye shall” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Peter 1:10 — a seven-word run found nowhere else in the Bible.
provenance.significance: 2 Peter 1:5-10 is a ladder of virtues to be added one to another — faith, virtue, knowledge, temperance, patience, godliness, brotherly kindness, charity — closed by the promise that whoever does these things shall never fall. Alma 37:33-37 is a list of the same shape and length, delivered as instructions to a son: preach repentance and faith, teach humility, teach meekness, never be weary of good works, learn wisdom, cry unto God, let thy doings be unto the Lord, counsel the Lord, lie down unto the Lord, rise with thanks. The seven-word run arrives at the end of it, exactly where 2 Peter's does, and the promise it introduces is changed from a negative to a positive: not 'ye shall never fall' but 'ye shall be lifted up at the last day'. The suppressed correspondence is that the source's guarantee is against falling, and the Book of Mormon's is about resurrection.

37:37.note: 'And if ye do these things, ye shall be lifted up at the last day.' The longest exact run in the chapter and a KJV singleton at seven words, closing a catalogue of virtues in the position 2 Peter closes one. Held at moderate rather than high because the run is entirely made of common words and could be arrived at independently; what argues against coincidence is its placement — it is the clause that discharges a list, in both texts. The n-gram stream ranked this highest in the chapter (rarity 3.50) and for once the ranking is right.
